routes.description: Establish a historically credible body of postmortem-appearance data, defend supernatural events as admissible historical conclusions, and show that resurrection explains the relevant data better than the principal naturalistic alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the appearance traditions are sufficiently established, resurrection has greater comparative explanatory adequacy than rival accounts, and neither methodological naturalism nor uncertainty about the precise divine agent blocks the supernatural conclusion.

motionBridge.description: The historical evidence and relevant background information must make Jesus's resurrection the best explanation of the reported postmortem appearances.

centralBridges.description: Early and corroborated sources must establish individual, hostile, and group appearance claims as data requiring explanation.
Resurrection must provide greater explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and economy than hallucination or other naturalistic alternatives.
Historical inquiry must be able to recognize an event transcending known natural capacities without first identifying its precise supernatural agent.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Independent allegedly paranormal phenomena may supply background plausibility for admitting supernatural explanations.
Reliable ordinary testimonial evidence must be capable in principle of supporting an extraordinary historical event.

routes.description: Maintain that resurrection proponents bear the evidential burden, challenge the accessibility and reliability of the ancient appearance reports, and deny that unexplained events or defeated natural alternatives establish supernatural causation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the historical data remain insufficiently confirmed or if resurrection and divine agency cannot be warranted from those data, making suspension of belief appropriate without requiring proof that resurrection was impossible.

motionBridge.description: Belief in Jesus's resurrection must be withheld unless the affirmative evidence establishes both the alleged event and the inferential move to resurrection.

centralBridges.description: Ancient appearance reports must provide accessible, independently supportable evidence adequate to establish the claimed postmortem events.
An unexplained or anomalous event must not be treated as evidence of supernatural causation without a method that distinguishes that cause from error, fraud, hallucination, or unknown natural causes.
The resurrection hypothesis must supply testable or discriminating explanatory content rather than merely relabeling the absence of a natural explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: The evidential limits created by two millennia of investigative distance must constrain comparisons with directly observable modern anomalies.
Attributing resurrection to divine action requires independent grounds for a capable and willing agent or evidence that itself discriminates in favor of such an agent.

sections.title: Historical foundation for the appearance claims
sections.rationale: The existence, independence, accessibility, and reliability of the Pauline, apostolic, individual, and group appearance traditions determine what historical data the competing explanations must address.

sections.title: Resurrection versus naturalistic explanations
sections.rationale: The motion turns centrally on whether resurrection explains the asserted historical data better than hallucination, error, dishonesty, or other naturalistic possibilities under comparative explanatory criteria.

sections.title: From anomaly to supernatural causation
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether an event judged incompatible with known natural capacities may be classified as supernatural or whether that classification merely substitutes a label for unresolved causation.

sections.title: Historical method and standards for extraordinary claims
sections.rationale: The parties' competing standards for testimony, repeatability, methodological naturalism, and investigation determine what kinds of evidence can justify an extraordinary historical conclusion.

sections.title: Background supernaturalism and identification of divine agency
sections.rationale: Allegedly paranormal phenomena and the question of prior grounds for God affect the background plausibility of resurrection and the further inference from a postmortem event to purposeful divine action.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Multiple classes of allegedly paranormal experience collectively provide empirical support for a supernatural dimension of reality.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Licona immediately before this uninterrupted opening-statement segment, and the speaker explicitly identifies his first major contention.

response.rationale: This is a constructive opening contention supplying purported background evidence for supernaturalism, so it has no earlier opposing demand to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly introduces the contention and promised evidential categories, though the excerpt only begins their development.

precisionFindings.rationale: The cumulative empirical-support claim is recoverable and qualified as suggestive, but the meaning and boundaries of supernatural dimension remain partly unsettled.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The phrase strongly suggests stops short of certainty, but the selected evidence announces four lines without displaying enough representative support for that force.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Cumulative evidence could raise background plausibility, but the bridge from heterogeneous experiences to a supernatural dimension is materially compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt promises four empirical lines but provides no representative cases, verification safeguards, independence analysis, or comparison with ordinary alternatives.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the designated subsidiary background-supernaturalism bridge and sits toward the upper portion of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move presents affirmative background evidence and does not meaningfully interpret a live opposing alternative in the selected material.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona expressly says empirical data strongly suggests a supernatural dimension and announces four supporting lines, beginning with paranormal experiences.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Early Pauline material and apostolic corroboration support a historical bedrock of individual, hostile, and group resurrection-appearance experiences.
moves.attributionBasis: This remains within Licona's uninterrupted opening statement, and the speaker expressly transitions to his second major contention concerning historical data.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the affirmative's asserted historical data through Paul, apostolic contact, and individual and group appearance experiences.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly identifies sources, a corroboration claim, and the historical facts that subsequent explanations must address.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical-bedrock proposition and source relationships are clear, but virtually undisputed scholarship and group-experience scope require bounded qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The source claims support a historical core, but virtually undisputed and the transition from beliefs to appearances slightly exceed the excerpt's demonstrated warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from early eyewitness-linked testimony and apostolic agreement to a historical appearance bedrock is coherent, with one bounded independence bridge implicit.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Paul's eyewitness claim and contact with disciples are specific support, but independence, transmission, and the evidential basis for group appearances remain compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly supplies the central historical-bedrock requirement and defines nearly all of the appearance data that the comparative route relies upon.

representationalCharity.rationale: This is an affirmative source argument rather than a developed treatment of a competing interpretation of the Pauline and apostolic material.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt identifies Paul as early, eyewitness-claiming, acquainted with disciples, and preaching their message, then states individual and group experiences.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Under explanatory scope, power, plausibility, and avoidance of ad hoc assumptions, resurrection explains the asserted historical bedrock better than hallucination.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted Licona opening continues through a methodological comparison and ends with his stated conclusion followed by audience applause.

response.rationale: This constructive move introduces comparative explanatory criteria and applies them to hallucination as the leading naturalistic rival to resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it provides a usable comparison with a named rival, though several criteria and alternative variants receive compressed treatment.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criteria and comparative conclusion are recoverable and stable, while the relevant variants of hallucination and background assumptions remain implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move offers genuine comparative reasons, but confidently favoring resurrection requires fuller treatment of rival variants, priors, and the asserted group data.

charity.alternative: Hallucination can explain experiences without requiring grief in every percipient or one literally shared hallucination.
charity.decisiveQualification: The hostile-Paul and group-report data still impose additional explanatory demands on any hallucination account.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The criteria form a coherent inference-to-best-explanation framework, but expected grief and group hallucination assumptions leave a material rival-model bridge underdeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named facts are applied to a recognized rival, yet psychological support, group-report verification, base rates, and alternative naturalistic accounts are not substantively defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the indispensable comparative-explanation bridge by naming criteria and applying them to the principal discussed rival.

representationalCharity.rationale: The comparison acknowledges hallucination's scope and economy but treats its strongest variants too narrowly and leaves their qualifications underdeveloped.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona grants hallucination explanatory scope and low ad hocness but challenges its power for Paul and groups while invoking plausibility and comparative criteria.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Belief in resurrection should be withheld unless its proponents discharge their evidential burden and show that the skeptical default is false.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives the floor to Matt Dillahunty, who identifies his position as being unconvinced and develops the null-hypothesis framework.

components.text: Whether resurrection is actually shown superior to the skeptical default under the proposed comparison.
Whether the asserted historical appearance evidence discharges the proponent's evidential burden.

response.rationale: The null-hypothesis framework contacts the demand that proponents establish superiority, but it does not yet examine whether the stated Pauline evidence meets that burden.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer: it contacts the decisive comparative burden while leaving the concrete historical premises and Licona's criteria largely unevaluated.

precisionFindings.rationale: The withholding rule is clear, but null hypothesis shifts between a practical default, an unconfirmed proposition, and an innocence analogy without full specification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Assigning proponents the burden is well matched, but describing the null as assumed true rather than retained provisionally is a slight overstatement.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The burden principle is coherent, but assuming the null true because it cannot be confirmed blurs withholding belief with affirming a contrary proposition.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The legal analogy illustrates burden allocation, but no independent defense is given for mapping null-hypothesis practice exactly onto this historical claim.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move expressly states the con motion-level completion rule: belief remains withheld until the affirmative shows its explanation superior.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move establishes an evidential default and does not yet render a substantive interpretation of Licona's strongest evidence or comparison.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty defines the null as the practical default and requires the affirmative proposal to demonstrate its superiority by showing that default false.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Reports of unexplained experiences do not establish a supernatural realm when that category remains poorly defined, unconfirmed, and causally uninvestigated.
moves.attributionBasis: This is an uninterrupted part of Dillahunty's opening, marked by first-person references to his magician background and his skeptical methodological position.

components.text: Whether reported paranormal experiences confirm a coherent supernatural dimension rather than unexplained phenomena.

response.rationale: The move directly disputes the paranormal-evidence inference by challenging confirmation, definition, and causal testing of the supernatural category.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive inference from anomaly reports to supernatural reality, though the excerpt gives limited engagement with particular cases.

precisionFindings.rationale: The criticism consistently distinguishes reported or unexplained experiences from confirmation of a defined supernatural category and states its epistemic scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move withholds confirmation rather than asserting impossibility and ties that restraint to definitional and investigative limitations stated in the excerpt.

charity.alternative: Multiple independently investigated anomalous classes could cumulatively support supernaturalism without individually proving it.
charity.decisiveQualification: Cumulative support still requires a sufficiently defined category and evidence connecting the anomalies to that category.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference is clear: poorly defined and unconfirmed causal categories cannot be established merely from reports of unexplained experiences.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological objections are relevant, but the excerpt does not examine representative paranormal cases or demonstrate that all announced evidence lacks safeguards.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly attacks the subsidiary background-supernaturalism bridge by contesting both the category and the inference from reported anomalies.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism fairly targets confirmation and causal linkage, although it does not separately assess the strongest evidence within each announced class.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty says supernatural reality has not been confirmed or demonstrated under testing and identifies poor definition as the first problem.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Eliminating a hoax or lacking a natural explanation does not establish resurrection, because attributing the event to divine action supplies no mechanism or explanatory content.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty remains the uninterrupted speaker and explicitly applies his earlier methodological criticism to resurrection arguments and an apologetic dichotomy.

components.text: Whether resurrection's comparative victory supplies explanatory content rather than merely naming an unresolved cause.

response.rationale: The move expressly diagnoses the inference's failure: eliminating hoax or natural explanation does not confer explanatory content on divine resurrection, so comparative labeling is insufficient.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely attacks the decisive explanatory inference and states the defeating consequence that saying God did it leaves the mystery unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The explanatory-content criticism is readily recoverable and consistently stated, with an implicit restriction to explanations lacking mechanisms or discriminating content.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The demand for discriminating content is warranted, but saying supernatural explanation has no explanatory power categorically slightly exceeds the demonstrated premise.

charity.alternative: A personal-agent hypothesis can explain purposive events without specifying a physical mechanism.
charity.decisiveQualification: It must still identify predictions or evidence that discriminate resurrection by that agent from other unknown causes.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The gap from excluding some natural accounts to affirming divine resurrection is correctly identified, though explanation need not always include a detailed mechanism.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The empty-tomb example and missing-content challenge support the critique, but the move does not test all explanatory predictions claimed for resurrection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly supplies the central con requirement that resurrection have testable or discriminating content rather than relabeling ignorance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move identifies the key missing discriminator but equates all divine-agent explanation with empty magic too broadly, weakening the strongest alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty asks how God raising Jesus became most plausible and argues that appeal to a larger mystery supplies no explanatory content.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Treating resurrection as plausible presupposes independent grounds for a God capable of and willing to raise Jesus, while private revelation is unverifiable hearsay to outsiders.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted skeptical opening continues, with the speaker contrasting theological and philosophical approaches before identifying their required divine premise.

components.text: Whether resurrection can be comparatively plausible without independent support for a capable and willing divine agent.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the background-plausibility component of the comparative inference by requiring support for an agent capable of and disposed toward resurrection.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts a decisive prior-plausibility issue explicitly, though it does not address the pro side's paranormal evidence as a possible source of such support.

precisionFindings.rationale: The prior-agent requirement is clear and its capable-and-desirous terms are stable, although the degree of prior support required remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Agent characteristics plainly affect plausibility, but claiming one must already believe in that agent overstates what a Bayesian comparative argument strictly requires.

charity.alternative: The resurrection evidence itself could raise the probability of a capable purposive agent without prior proof.
charity.decisiveQualification: That evidence must discriminate such agency from unknown natural causes and other possible agents.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A capable and willing agent is relevant to resurrection plausibility, but requiring prior belief rather than prior probability creates a material overstrong conditional.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt invokes another debater's acknowledged premise but offers little independent support for the stronger claim that prior agent belief is necessary.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the subsidiary theistic-background bridge by specifying the capable-and-willing agent premise needed for divine attribution.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move highlights a real prior-probability issue but states it as a required antecedent belief, underplaying evidential feedback from the event itself.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty states that resurrection arguments presuppose a God who exists and is capable of and desirous of resurrection, calling this a necessary component.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Neither historical inquiry nor science can confirm supernatural causation without a workable account of what the supernatural is and how it causally operates.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty remains the sole speaker and explicitly turns from the limits of direct scientific investigation to the historical method used by Licona.

components.text: Whether historical comparison can establish supernatural causation without a workable account of that causal category.
Whether attributed supernatural claims can be investigated as events despite uncertainty about their cause.

response.rationale: The move contacts both investigation and causal attribution, conceding that attributed claims can be investigated while denying a causal connection absent a positive account.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly addresses the decisive methodological inference and carefully separates investigating an attributed claim from confirming its proposed supernatural cause.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly distinguishes event investigation from causal confirmation and expressly conditions the latter on understanding what supernatural means positively.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The demand for a method linking evidence to the asserted causal category fits the conclusion, without claiming that anomalous events themselves are uninvestigable.

charity.alternative: History may infer an extraordinary cause abductively without experimentally modeling its mechanism.
charity.decisiveQualification: The abductive hypothesis still needs identifiable content that differentiates it from fraud, error, or unknown natural causation.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between investigating reported events and confirming a supernatural causal connection is explicit, consistent, and directly resolves a likely equivocation.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The methodological distinction is well supported conceptually, though the universal inability claim receives no comparison with successful historical agent inferences.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move nearly maximally supports the central causal-underdetermination bridge by demanding a method linking evidence to supernatural causation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move fairly permits investigation of attributed claims and reserves its objection for the unestablished causal link, preserving the strongest alternative's legitimate scope.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty permits investigation of claims attributed to supernatural causes but denies causal confirmation until the category and its operations are understood.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Scientific and historical disciplines use different investigative methods, so lack of controlled repeatability does not by itself disqualify supernatural claims from investigation.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Licona, who explicitly frames the passage as his rebuttal to Dillahunty's opening objections.

components.text: Whether lack of a single repeatable scientific test prevents disciplined investigation of supernatural claims.
Whether the announced paranormal evidence can be tested by methods appropriate to its evidential discipline.

response.rationale: The response directly contests the alleged methodological bar by distinguishing discipline-specific methods, but only partly answers the demand for causal discrimination.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts investigation and testing, while leaving the decisive request for a workable supernatural causal link substantially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The discipline-specific-method proposition is clear and stable, though which historical controls suffice for causal supernatural conclusions remains implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The modest claim that controlled repeatability is not the only investigative method is well matched, with the sufficiency of alternatives left unstated.

charity.alternative: The skeptical objection permits historical investigation but demands a method that identifies supernatural causation.
charity.decisiveQualification: Different disciplinary methods answer the investigation issue but do not by themselves establish that missing causal discriminator.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Different disciplines plainly can employ different methods, but that fact alone does not show that any available method warrants the supernatural attribution.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Named paranormal categories illustrate the intended domain, yet the excerpt gives no specific historical safeguards or successful validation procedure.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The reply attacks the central causal-underdetermination bridge, but it reaches only the investigability component rather than the full causal-discrimination demand.

representationalCharity.rationale: Licona correctly rejects a universal laboratory-test demand but partially compresses Dillahunty's more careful distinction between investigating claims and confirming causes.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona lists paranormal phenomena, near-death experiences, apparitions, and answered prayer, then argues disciplines have different methods and no single scientific method.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Methodological naturalism can exclude supernatural explanations in advance and prevent recognition of events that known natural causes cannot plausibly explain.
moves.attributionBasis: Licona continues his rebuttal in a sustained first-person critique, with no speaker transition before the next topic.

components.text: Whether methodological rules exclude a supernatural explanation before comparative historical assessment can occur.
Whether a highly specific anomalous disclosure can favor supernatural causation over hallucination.

response.rationale: The move challenges prior exclusion and supplies a private-information hypothetical, but it does not fully furnish the positive causal method Dillahunty requested.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the exclusion concern and provides discriminating evidence, while leaving definition and causal-operation requirements underdeveloped.

precisionFindings.rationale: The anti-exclusion claim is recoverable, but miracle, supernatural event, and least-probable explanation are not cleanly distinguished in the hypothetical.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The hypothetical makes ordinary alternatives less plausible, but it does not alone warrant calling supernatural causation more probable than every unknown alternative.

charity.alternative: Methodological naturalism can investigate the disclosure while withholding a supernatural causal verdict.
charity.decisiveQualification: Withholding is not prior exclusion if the proposed cause lacks independently discriminating content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Prior exclusion can bias comparison, but the move risks a false choice between supernatural causation and group hallucination without exhausting other explanations.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The private-conversation scenario is evidentially suggestive but hypothetical and does not establish verification, fraud controls, or a unique supernatural causal link.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports the central supernatural-admissibility requirement by arguing that supernatural hypotheses must not be excluded before comparison.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response exposes a risk of dogmatic exclusion but treats the skeptical position too readily as choosing any natural account regardless of evidence.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona uses a private-information apparition hypothetical and argues that automatically preferring hallucination or any natural account exemplifies methodological naturalism.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: Case-by-case comparison of hypotheses using the historical data and relevant background information favors resurrection over the proposed naturalistic alternatives.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage remains Licona's uninterrupted rebuttal and repeatedly restates his historical-hypothesis methodology in the first person.

components.text: Whether disciplined comparison can show resurrection more probable than naturalistic hypotheses.
Whether the affirmative has a method for showing its hypothesis superior to the skeptical default.
Whether historical inquiry has a controlled procedure for evaluating competing causal hypotheses.

response.rationale: The response supplies a comparative historical procedure and asserts its result, directly contacting burden and method, but compresses the promised all-rival application.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive comparative demand but only asserts that resurrection wins against all other naturalistic hypotheses without presenting those comparisons.

precisionFindings.rationale: The case-by-case comparative procedure is clear, but all naturalistic hypotheses and relevant background information remain broadly scoped and implicitly bounded.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Saying resurrection comes out on top every time materially exceeds the excerpt, which applies the framework expressly only to hallucination and supplies no uncertainty.

charity.alternative: Naturalistic rivals may be weak individually while the residual category of error, legend, or unknown cause remains collectively significant.
charity.decisiveQualification: A best-explanation conclusion requires comparison with serious rival combinations and relevant prior plausibility.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The historical-comparison framework is coherent, but the universal conclusion is supported by an asserted rather than displayed series of comparisons.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The excerpt names data, hypothesis formulation, and probability weighing, yet gives results only by assertion beyond the previously sketched hallucination case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This is direct motion-level contact because it expressly claims resurrection is the best explanation after case-by-case comparison with naturalistic rivals.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move invokes all alternatives but does not articulate their strongest forms or the residual uncertainty, materially weakening the competing case.

moves.evidenceBasis: Licona advocates controlled historical comparison of hypotheses against known data and says resurrection defeats all naturalistic hypotheses, while acknowledging only hallucination was shown.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Methodological naturalism permits investigation of extraordinary events but withholds supernatural attribution until a testable model distinguishes genuine phenomena from fraud, error, and hallucination.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator announces Dillahunty's rebuttal, after which he directly answers Licona's claims in a continuous monologue.

components.text: Whether methodological naturalism bars testing extraordinary claims or instead withholds only unsupported causal attribution.
Whether discipline-specific investigation answers the need to confirm a supernatural causal model.
Whether comparative historical assessment alone justifies supernatural attribution.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses Licona's exclusion objection as mistaken: claims remain testable, while attribution is withheld pending confirmation and discrimination.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive methodological premise, preserves investigation, and states the defeating consequence for premature supernatural attribution.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between testing extraordinary events and confirming supernatural causation is explicit, stable, and carefully limited to current methodological ability.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The withholding rule is proportionate to the stated absence of confirmed causal discrimination and does not claim that extraordinary events cannot occur.

charity.alternative: Methodological naturalism may become dogmatic if it refuses any evidence capable of supporting nonnatural agency.
charity.decisiveQualification: The stated rule allows testing and changes only when a confirmed model distinguishes the proposed cause from fraud, error, and hallucination.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The event-versus-cause distinction is explicit and consistently defeats the charge that methodological naturalism prevents investigation altogether.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The comet illustration and stated confirmation standard concretely support openness to testing, with only the precise threshold for causal confirmation left compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly and strongly supports the central causal-underdetermination bridge through a test-before-attribution requirement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply handles the strongest exclusion concern by expressly allowing investigation and reserving judgment only on the unsupported causal label.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty says methodological naturalism does not bar testing attributed claims, but supernatural appeal must await investigation and confirmation of that causal category.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Paul is a weak foundation for resurrection because he lacked direct access to Jesus's ministry, death, burial, and empty tomb, while surviving reports do not independently demonstrate a return from death.
moves.attributionBasis: The first-person skeptical assessment remains part of Dillahunty's announced rebuttal and ends immediately before the moderator changes formats.

components.text: Whether Paul provides direct and independently adequate evidence for Jesus's death, burial, empty tomb, and postmortem return.

response.rationale: The response directly attacks the asserted Pauline foundation by identifying Paul's lack of direct access to Jesus's life, death, burial, and tomb.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts source sufficiency, though it does not answer Licona's separate claim that Paul knew disciples and transmitted their appearance tradition.

precisionFindings.rationale: Paul's limitations are clearly stated, but the move partly conflates lack of eyewitness access to earlier events with weakness regarding Paul's own claimed experience.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The argument presents source limitations as reasons for evidential weakness rather than proof of falsity and acknowledges Paul's scholarly status as the best source.

charity.alternative: Paul can be early and valuable because he claims an experience and knew leading disciples despite missing Jesus's ministry.
charity.decisiveQualification: That value does not make him a direct witness to the death, burial, tomb, or other people's experiences.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from lack of direct access to reduced support for several historical claims is sound, with Paul's own experience requiring separate treatment.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move names specific absences in Paul's access and concedes his relative source status, but does not analyze the content or dating of his reports.

relevanceBurden.rationale: This directly attacks the central historical-bedrock bridge by challenging the affirmative's principal early source and its evidential reach.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response grants Paul may be the best source and accurately isolates his limitations, though it omits fuller engagement with apostolic corroboration.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty concedes Paul may be the best source, then notes he never met the living Jesus and did not witness the death, burial, or empty tomb.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Calling an event supernatural merely labels the absence of a natural explanation and cannot justify specific conclusions about gods, spirits, souls, or resurrection.
moves.attributionBasis: Within the alternating questioning, Dillahunty explicitly identifies the repeated explanatory pattern and develops a continuous skeptical challenge.

components.text: Whether inability to fit an event within known natural explanations positively identifies a supernatural cause.
Whether gaps in currently available natural explanations make resurrection the best causal verdict.

response.rationale: The move directly challenges the inference from currently unaccounted-for phenomena to a supernatural label and questions the supposed impossibility of group explanations.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive inference from failed known explanations to supernatural causation, though the excerpt is less explicit about specific gods or agents.

precisionFindings.rationale: The based-on-what-we-know limitation clearly bounds the objection and maintains a stable distinction between unexplained and supernaturally caused.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The conclusion is limited to causal underdetermination under current knowledge and does not assert that a supernatural cause is impossible.

charity.alternative: An event genuinely impossible under natural laws could definitionally be called supernatural without identifying an agent.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical evidence must establish actual impossibility, not merely failure of presently proposed natural explanations.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The move coherently separates inability to account for an event using current knowledge from a positive supernatural causal conclusion.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The repeated-form critique is well targeted, but the selected evidence does not fully document which group-experience alternatives are empirically possible.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move strongly supports central causal underdetermination by denying that failure of known natural accounts identifies a supernatural cause.

representationalCharity.rationale: The criticism preserves the distinction between current explanatory limits and demonstrated natural impossibility, which is the strongest relevant qualification.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty emphasizes the repeated move from cannot currently account for this to a causal conclusion and disputes claims about what hallucinations can do.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: The claim that Jesus appeared to five hundred people lacks accessible identities, statements, and experiences sufficient to investigate whether the reported event occurred.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly invites Dillahunty's comment, and his first-person response continues until the moderator resumes speaking.

components.text: Whether the reported appearance to five hundred is accessible and sufficiently evidenced to count as historical group data.
Whether group hallucination must be explained before the underlying five-hundred-person report is established.

response.rationale: The move directly shifts the evidential demand from explaining a mass experience to first establishing an investigable report through identities and testimony.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It expressly contacts both the group-data premise and the downstream hallucination comparison, identifying the prior verification step those arguments require.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim is narrowly limited to this five-hundred report and identifies the missing identities, access, investigation, and sufficiency conditions.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker states personal evidential insufficiency rather than categorical falsity and ties it to the inability to investigate the reported group.

charity.alternative: An early named-source report can carry some evidential weight even when most witnesses are not individually preserved.
charity.decisiveQualification: Its weight remains limited without accessible identities, independent statements, or details sufficient to test the group claim.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The priority inference is strong: one need not explain a 500-person hallucination until sufficiently reliable evidence establishes the reported event.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The specific absence of accessible witnesses and statements supports the investigative criticism, with only the surviving report's residual evidential value compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports central source sufficiency by challenging a major group-appearance datum at its evidential foundation.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not deny all weight to the report; it fairly argues that the extraordinary numerical claim cannot bear the proposed explanatory load.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty calls the five-hundred report extraordinary, notes there is no way to investigate it, and prioritizes establishing occurrence over hallucination analysis.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: An extraordinary event does not require a special category of extraordinary evidence when sufficiently good ordinary eyewitness evidence supports it.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator offers Licona a reply, and Licona develops his beheading hypothetical until Dillahunty answers his distinction between event and evidence.

components.text: Whether extraordinary events require a special evidential category beyond sufficiently good eyewitness testimony.
Whether the actual ancient testimony is sufficiently accessible and reliable to establish the claimed group event.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the general evidential-standard issue through a vivid eyewitness hypothetical but does not answer the concrete accessibility defects in the ancient reports.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer addresses the standard in principle while leaving the decisive application to Paul's five-hundred report and source quality unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between extraordinary event and good ordinary evidence is recoverable, but ordinary and extraordinary evidence remain conversationally contested and underdefined.

moves.speaker: Matt Dillahunty
moves.proposition: Even observing an extraordinary return from death would justify accepting that the event occurred without justifying an unsupported supernatural causal explanation.
moves.attributionBasis: Dillahunty initiates the event-versus-explanation distinction and repeatedly returns to it, although brief Licona interjections occur within the exchange.

components.text: Whether observing or accepting an extraordinary event also warrants the proposed supernatural causal explanation.
Whether openness to the event entails accepting supernatural causation rather than withholding causal judgment.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses a conflation between event occurrence and causal explanation and states that accepting the former does not justify the latter.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly contacts the decisive inference, articulates the event-cause distinction, and states the defeating consequence for supernatural attribution.

precisionFindings.rationale: Despite brief interjections, the proposition remains clear: acceptance of occurrence is distinct from acceptance of an unsupported causal explanation.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The refusal is limited to an unjustified causal explanation and expressly allows belief that the extraordinary event happened.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between accepting an observed event and accepting a proposed explanation is explicit, consistent, and defeats the alleged implication.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The shared hypothetical strongly demonstrates the logical distinction, with the remaining gap concerning what evidence could eventually establish natural impossibility.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move nearly maximally supports central causal underdetermination by separating event evidence from an unsupported supernatural causal verdict.

representationalCharity.rationale: The response correctly preserves event acceptance and focuses its objection on causal overreach, though it treats the supernatural label mainly as ignorance.

moves.evidenceBasis: Dillahunty says he would believe the extraordinary return occurred but would reject the causal explanation absent justification, calling supernatural a bucket for ignorance.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona
moves.proposition: A verified event impossible under known natural laws may be classified as supernatural even when its particular causal agent remains unidentified.
moves.attributionBasis: The transcript explicitly introduces Licona, whose uninterrupted first-person answer continues until Dillahunty responds at the next row.

components.text: Whether an event established as impossible under natural laws may be classified as supernatural before identifying its agent.
Whether failure to identify God, angel, demon, or another agent prevents classifying the event itself.
Whether the event classification supplies a workable method for proving impossibility under natural laws.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the event-versus-agent distinction and concedes agent uncertainty, but it assumes rather than supplies the method establishing natural impossibility.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer directly resolves agent identification after impossibility is verified while leaving the decisive verification and causal-discrimination demand unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conditional proposition is clearly bounded to verified natural impossibility and expressly separates event classification from identification of the particular agent.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Given the speaker's stipulated definition, the conditional classification follows, and uncertainty about God, angels, demons, or extraterrestrials is explicit.

charity.alternative: Supernatural may only rename established natural inexplicability and still fail to identify any positive cause.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The conditional distinction between a law-transcending event and its unknown agent is coherent, with the proof of natural impossibility left external.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The definitional reasoning supports classification under the stipulated antecedent, but no evidence or method establishes that antecedent in the resurrection case.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The move directly supports central supernatural admissibility by arguing that agent uncertainty need not block classifying a verified law-transcending event.

moves.speaker: Mike Licona

components.text: Whether resurrection evidence may itself support supernaturalism and theism without prior proof of God.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the prior-support premise while leaving the decisive inference from a resurrection event to probable theism largely asserted.
